title: Due Diligence: STR-Specific Inspections, Appraisal & Title Review

slides.title: Test the house and the rental business before your contingency windows close
slides.subtitle: Lesson PA.9. Due Diligence: STR-Specific Inspections, Appraisal & Title Review
meta: Education only. Not legal, lending, or insurance advice.
slides.notes:
This lesson starts the day your offer is accepted. You have a house under contract and a short window to find out what you actually bought.

I'm going to show you how to spend that window. We'll test the building, and we'll test the rental business Sam underwrote in PA.4. Then we'll rerun his numbers with what we found.

By the end you'll have two things. A filled diligence tracker, and a dated decision: proceed, renegotiate, or walk.

We'll use Cedar Ridge the whole way. Maya and Chris have it under contract at $385,000. Every finding I show you on Cedar Ridge is made up for teaching, and I'll flag it on the slide. None of this is legal, lending, or insurance advice. Your attorney, inspector, insurer, and lender confirm the real answers for your address.

slides.title: Order the diligence work by what can kill the deal fastest
slides.text: Your contract sets the windows. Put every deadline in a calendar the day you sign.

nodes.d: No repair fixes a ban or an uninsurable house.
Read the commitment with your attorney.
The lender orders it. You know when it's due.

box.label: This fails if
box.text: You find a problem after a contingency expires. It's still your problem, and most of your bargaining power is gone.

slides.notes:
Your accepted offer from PA.8 bought you time. That time is the real asset in this phase.

Most purchase contracts give you a window to inspect and a window to secure financing. Some add a separate appraisal contingency. The names and lengths come from your contract and your state's forms.

The CFPB puts it plainly. With a satisfactory-inspection contingency, you should be able to cancel without penalty if serious flaws turn up. That protection works only while the window is open, and only in the form your contract states.

So order the work by what can kill the deal fastest. Legal use and the insurance quote go first. Inspections come next, because specialists book up. Title and survey run alongside.

Open one folder for the property on day one. Every report, quote, email, and photo goes in with a date in the file name. You'll use that folder again at closing in PA.11 and in the handoff in PA.12.

slides.title: Diligence asks two questions: is the house sound, and can it run the business?

left.head: Is the house sound?
items: Roof, HVAC, water, septic, electrical
A general inspector plus specialists
Findings become repair costs

right.head: Can it run Sam's business?
right.note: At his guest count and his price.
items: Legal STR use for this exact parcel
An insurer willing to cover 8 guests on a lake
Real guest capacity
Answered by the county and the insurer, in writing

box.label: How to read your PA.4 package
box.text: Treat the underwriting as a guess to test. Every finding confirms a line or changes it. At the end you rerun the numbers.

slides.notes:
A regular homebuyer asks one question during diligence. Is this house sound? You have to ask a second one. Can this house run the rental business in Sam's underwriting, at his guest count and his price?

Those two questions need different people. An inspector can tell you the roof has four years left. Only the county can tell you whether it will issue a rental permit. Only the insurer can tell you whether it will cover eight guests on a lake.

Your tracker names each owner in writing.

Bring your PA.4 underwriting package from Sam's lesson into this one. Base case and weak case. We're going to treat it as a hypothesis. Every finding either confirms a line or changes it, and at the end we rerun it.

slides.title: Hand the inspector a ten-item STR list, because guests work a house harder
rows: Age, remaining life, flashing, gutters, signs of past leaks in the attic
Age, service history, capacity for the full house, remote setting and monitoring
On a private well, the water test is on you. Test during the contingency.
Pump the tank, check baffles and drain field, get the permitted bedroom count
A lender may require a pest certificate. Check wood near water for rot and insects.
Panel condition, capacity for a hot tub or EV charger, GFCI near water
Winter access for a cleaner, who plows, parking for the guest count
Drain covers that meet federal standards (CPSC)
Smoke and CO alarms, exits from every sleeping room, extinguishers
Look up the address on the FEMA flood map. Flood is a separate policy.
slides.caption: Every finding gets a written cost range. Record the midpoint in your tracker.
slides.notes:
Start with a general home inspection. Check the inspector out yourself. The CFPB notes that some areas don't require inspectors to be licensed, and it suggests checking references and your state or county licensing authority.

Then tell the inspector the plan. Eight guests. Turnovers every few days. People who don't know the house.

This is the list I'd hand over for a house like Cedar Ridge. A roof near the end of its life is a capital expense you'll pay while guests are booked. Airbnb's own safety rules name blocked exits, inoperable smoke detectors, and exposed wiring as hazards hosts must address. FEMA says most homeowners insurance doesn't cover flood damage.

Add specialists for the systems a general inspector only looks at from the surface. And every finding gets a cost. Ask for a written range and put the midpoint in your tracker.

slides.title: Test the well and septic during the contingency, because after closing they're yours
items: The EPA says its public drinking water rules don't apply to private wells.
EPA suggests testing yearly for coliform bacteria, nitrates, dissolved solids, and pH. CDC says use certified labs.
EPA notes many states require a septic inspection when real estate transfers.
For a typical household, EPA suggests inspecting every 1 to 3 years and pumping every 3 to 5 years.
An STR isn't a typical household. More guests and more laundry mean more load.
Ask what bedroom count the septic was permitted for. The county health department usually holds the record.
slides.notes:
Lake houses often run on a private well and a septic tank. Both are easy to skip and expensive to find out about later.

On the well, the EPA is direct. Its public drinking water rules don't apply to private wells. The owner does the testing. EPA recommends yearly tests for coliform bacteria, nitrates, dissolved solids, and pH. The CDC recommends certified labs. Do the test during the contingency, not after closing.

On septic, EPA notes many states require an inspection at transfer. For a typical household it suggests inspecting every 1 to 3 years and pumping every 3 to 5. A rental with eight guests is not a typical household.

So ask the septic inspector for three things. Pump the tank. Inspect the baffles and the drain field. And tell you what bedroom count the system was permitted for. That last number comes back on the capacity slide.

slides.title: Five tests decide whether this exact address can run this business
rows: Zoning, permit category, any cap or waitlist, owner-tied permit (SR.1)
Does the permit transfer? Who honors stays booked after closing?
Do recorded covenants limit rentals or business use?
A bindable STR quote, its conditions, and their deadlines

box.label: Real capacity
box.text: Take the lowest of three limits: the septic permit's bedroom count, the permit's occupancy cap, and what the insurer will write. If it's below 8, your revenue line changes.

slides.notes:
A normal home inspection never touches this half.

First, legal use. You and Sam checked the market in PA.2. A market answer is not an address answer. Use the SR.1 checklist on this parcel, and get the licensing office's answer in writing if you can. Airbnb's own guidance says hosts are responsible for permits, zoning, safety, and health rules.

Second, transfer. Does the permit move to a new owner, or do you apply fresh? If there are bookings after your closing date, the contract says who honors them and who keeps the money. Don't rely on the listing agent's word.

Third, covenants. Cedar Ridge has no HOA. Recorded covenants can still limit rentals.

Fourth, a bindable insurance quote before the inspection window closes. Airbnb says AirCover isn't a substitute for your own policy.

Fifth, capacity. The lowest of the three limits is your real number.

slides.title: A clean appraisal says nothing about the septic, and a clean inspection says nothing about value

left.head: Home inspector
items: Looks for flaws
Check references and licensing yourself
Findings drive repairs and renegotiation

right.head: Appraiser
right.note: Independent. Estimates value for the lender.
items: Gives the lender a market value estimate
On a first-lien dwelling loan, you're entitled to a copy before closing
On a DSCR loan, ask if it includes a rent or income analysis

slides.notes:
The CFPB draws this line clearly. A home inspector works for you and looks for flaws. An appraiser is an independent professional whose job is to give the lender an estimate of market value.

So you need both, and neither one covers the other. A clean appraisal doesn't mean the septic works. A clean inspection doesn't mean the house is worth your price.

On a first-lien dwelling loan, you're entitled to a copy of the appraisal before closing. That's in the CFPB's version of Regulation B, section 1002.14. When it arrives, read the comparable sales. Don't just look at the final number.

If you're on a DSCR loan, ask one more question. Does the appraisal include a rent or income analysis, and which figure will the lender actually use? You want that answer before the report lands.

slides.title: A $375,000 appraisal would add $7,424 to Cedar Ridge's cash to close

lines.label: Loan at 75% of the lower value
Closing costs, with points down to $2,812

slides.side:
The canonical cash to close is $110,688. The low appraisal adds $7,424.

Lenders generally size the loan on the lower of price or appraised value. Confirm your lender's rule in writing.

side_box.label: Already decided
side_box.text: PA.8 worked the low-appraisal decision. Here you just need the cash effect the day the report lands.

slides.notes:
PA.8 already worked through what to do with a low appraisal. In diligence, your job is narrower. Know the cash effect the day the report lands.

Say Cedar Ridge appraises at $375,000. That's an assumption for teaching. Lenders generally size the loan on the lower of price or appraised value, so check your lender's rule in writing.

At 75%, the loan drops to $281,250. The price is still $385,000, so the down payment rises to $103,750. Points are 1% of a smaller loan, so they fall to $2,812. Closing costs become $14,362.

Cash to close comes to $118,112. That's $7,424 more than the canonical $110,688.

If you don't have $7,424 sitting unassigned, you want to know that before the appraisal comes back, not after.

slides.title: Anything in the title commitment's exceptions stays with the land after you buy
slides.text: Requirements list what must happen before the title company will insure. Exceptions list what the policy won't cover.
rows: An unpaid contractor or tax lien should be paid from the seller's proceeds at closing.
A neighbor's path to the lake changes privacy. A utility easement can limit a hot tub pad.
Read every recorded restriction for rental or business-use language.
Shows where lot lines, the dock, and the driveway actually sit.

box.label: Two title policies
box.text: The lender's policy covers only the loan, and most lenders require it. The owner's policy is optional and protects your equity. With about $96,000 of your own cash in, decide it on purpose.

slides.notes:
The title company searches public records and issues a title commitment. Read it yourself, with your attorney or closing agent. You're the one who knows how you plan to use the land.

Two parts matter. The requirements list what has to happen before the title company will insure, like paying off the seller's mortgage. The exceptions list what the policy won't cover. Anything in the exceptions stays with the land after you buy it.

The CFPB gives unpaid contractors and unpaid taxes as examples of claims owner's title insurance can protect against. It also lists survey fees among the closing services you can often shop for. A lake lot with a dock and shared access is reason enough to order a survey.

On the policies, the CFPB says most lenders require the lender's policy. The owner's policy is optional. I'd want it priced and decided on purpose. PA.11 shows where it lands on the closing figures.

slides.title: Every finding gets one of four decisions, written down with a reason that day

nodes.d: You'll live with it and budget for it.
The seller repairs before closing, with proof.
You terminate inside the contingency window.

box.label: Save the evidence
box.text: Every report, answer, and quote goes in the property folder. The insurer, lender, and permit office will ask for several of them again.

slides.notes:
The decision column in your tracker has only four possible answers.

Accept means you'll live with it and put it in the budget. Seller fixes means the seller repairs it before closing and shows you proof, like an invoice. Credit or price means you negotiate money. Walk means you terminate inside the contingency window.

Write the decision the day you make it, and write why. One sentence is enough. Three weeks later, when the lender asks why the septic line changed, you'll have the answer in your own words.

Save everything in the property folder. The insurer, the lender, and the permit office will each ask for some of the same documents again.

[Recording note: Preston can add a real example here if he has one.]

slides.title: Cedar Ridge's tracker names who verified each finding and what was decided
rows: Permitted. Doesn't transfer. Cap of 8 guests.
$3,200 / year. Railing and alarms within 30 days.
Loose posts on the dock stairs.
None on the lower sleeping level.
slides.caption: Selected rows. The full 13-row tracker, including septic program, survey, and bookings, is in PA.9.8.
slides.notes:
Here's Cedar Ridge. Maya and Chris have it under contract at $385,000 on the DSCR quote. Their PA.8 terms give them a 10-day inspection contingency, a 30-day financing contingency, an appraisal contingency, and a 45-day close. All of these findings are assumptions for teaching.

Look at the Verified by column first. Every row has a named source. The permit answer came from the county in writing, not from the listing agent.

The permit is allowed, but it doesn't transfer, so they apply as new owners. The insurer quoted $3,200 a year with two conditions: fix the dock railing and add lower-level alarms within 30 days.

The septic has a broken outlet baffle and no effluent filter. The well tested positive for total coliform. The title shows a $3,100 mechanic's lien and a footpath easement to the lake. The appraisal came in fine.

Now we turn these rows into money.

slides.title: Four findings add $3,820 a year that PA.4's generic lines don't cover
rows: Well UV lamp and annual water test

box.label: First rerun: all four on top
box.text: The cautious first rerun adds all four to B1's budget. That keeps the whole 5% capital reserve ($3,714) free for surprises.

slides.notes:
Four findings add costs that recur every year. PA.4's generic lines don't name them.

The roof needs replacing in about five years at $14,000. Spread that over five years and you set aside $2,800 a year. The septic needs a yearly inspection and more pumping because of the guest load. That's $400. The well's UV lamp and annual test are $220. And the county permit renewal is $400.

Total: $3,820 a year.

The first rerun is the cautious version. It stacks all four on top of the budget. That keeps the whole 5% capital reserve of $3,714 free for surprises. Hold on to that choice. We'll come back to it in two slides.

slides.title: The cautious first rerun cuts base-case cash flow from $5,572 to $1,752 a year
slides.caption: First rerun NOI: $29,209 - $3,820 = $25,389. Less $23,637 DSCR debt service = $1,752, about $146 a month. Weak case: $18,162 - $3,820 - $23,637 = -$9,295.
slides.notes:
Now rerun Sam's baseline with the $3,820 stacked on top.

The canonical base case had gross booking revenue of $74,275, operating costs of $45,066, and NOI of $29,209. Take off the $3,820 and NOI becomes $25,389.

The DSCR debt service is $23,637 a year. So annual cash flow drops from $5,572 to $1,752. That's about $146 a month instead of about $464.

The weak case gets worse by the same $3,820. Weak-case NOI was $18,162. Subtract the $3,820 and the debt service, and you get minus $9,295 a year, down from minus $5,475.

Revenue didn't change here, because real capacity stayed at 8. If the septic or the permit had capped them at 6, you'd rerun revenue first, before any of this.

slides.title: The first rerun breaks three written buy-box rules, and the rule says renegotiate or walk
slides.caption: PA.1's cash caps still pass: cash to close $110,688, cash to close plus furnishing $142,688, punch list $2,955 against a $4,000 limit.

box.label: Their written rule
box.text: A broken buy box means renegotiate or walk. The box changes only in writing. The seller had already refused a credit or a price cut.

slides.notes:
Cash isn't the only rule Maya and Chris brought into diligence. PA.1 and PA.8 wrote down three more, and PA.9 has to run them.

Base-case cash flow has to be at least $5,000. The first rerun gives $1,752. Fail.

The weak case can lose no more than $6,000 a year. The first rerun loses $9,295. Fail.

Base NOI has to be at least 1.20 times annual principal and interest. $25,389 over $23,637 is 1.07. Fail.

The cash caps from PA.1 still pass. Cash to close is still $110,688, and the $2,955 punch list is under their $4,000 limit.

So the written rule applies: renegotiate or walk. The box only changes in writing. The seller had already refused a credit or a price cut. Before walking, they reread their own budget.

slides.title: Funding the roof and routine upkeep from B1's reserve lines brings all three rules back
rows: Cost added on top of B1

box.label: Each cost counted once
box.text: Roof $2,800 from the 5% capital reserve. Septic $400 and UV lamp $220 from the 5% repairs line. Permit $400 on top. Less cushion for surprises.

slides.notes:
Here's what they found. B1 already sets aside 5% of gross as a capital reserve, $3,714 in the base case. That line exists for bills like a roof. B1 also has a 5% repairs line for routine upkeep. With the new baffle and filter in place, the septic program and the UV lamp are routine upkeep.

So the final budget counts each cost once. The $2,800 roof fund comes out of the capital reserve. The septic and UV costs come out of the repairs line. Only the $400 permit renewal is new, so only that goes on top.

Final NOI is $28,809. Base cash flow is $5,172, about $431 a month. The weak case is minus $5,875. Coverage is 1.22. All three rules pass, none by much. Base cash flow clears $5,000 by $172, and the weak case clears the limit by $125.

Here's the price. In the base case, the capital line has $914 left after the roof. In a weak year it has $66. Any other capital bill, like the 14-year-old HVAC, comes from the $15,342 property reserve.

slides.title: Seller repairs and the final budget turn a $1,575 cash shortfall into $7,265 spare
slides.text: The seller refused a $7,000 roof credit but agreed to fix the septic ($1,850) and treat the well ($2,000) before closing, and to pay the $3,100 lien.

box.label: What it did to the deal
box.text: $7,265 is $2,735 under their $10,000 floor from PA.8.6. Saving $3,500 a month refills it before the 45-day close. Cash-on-cash falls from 3.9% to 3.6%.

slides.notes:
Now the cash. PA.8 left Maya and Chris $11,020 unallocated, after their Test 3 set-asides. Those set-asides included two years of weak-case shortfall.

The first draft had the buyers paying every repair: $350, $1,650, $2,300, $380, and $275. That's $4,955. With the $3,820 stacked on top, the weak-case shortfall grows by $7,640 over the two years PA.8 funds. Together that's $12,595 against $11,020. The deal fails by $1,575.

So they renegotiated inside the 10-day window. The seller refused a $7,000 roof credit, but agreed to repair the septic and treat the well before closing, and to pay the lien. Now the buyers pay only $2,955. That column passes by $425.

On the final budget, the weak case is only $400 a year worse than planned, so the extra reserve is $800. The total is $3,755, and $7,265 stays unallocated. That's under the $10,000 floor they set in PA.8.6 by $2,735. They still save $3,500 a month, so the 45 days to closing refill it.

Base-case cash-on-cash falls from 3.9% to 3.6%. That's $5,172 over $145,643.

slides.text: Proceed and walk can both be right. Write the decision before the deadline, not after.
slides.support: Maya and Chris proceeded, with the reserve change in writing. One more rule: if year one runs near the weak case, they revisit co-host and pricing at OP.11's 12-month review.
slides.notes:
So what did they decide?

The house is sound enough to buy. The final budget meets all three buy-box rules and the cash test, each with a thin margin.

Maya and Chris decided to proceed. They wrote down why: B1's reserve lines fund the roof and the routine septic and well costs. The permit is the only new cost. They also wrote a new rule. If the first 12 months run closer to the weak case, they revisit the co-host and pricing plan at the 12-month review in OP.11.

A buyer with less cash could read the same file and walk inside the 10-day window. So could a buyer who wants the whole capital reserve kept free for surprises. That would also be a sound decision.

What makes either answer defensible is timing. Both are written down, with a reason, before the deadline. The bad version is the one where nobody decides and the window just closes.
slides.title: Proceed or walk can both be right if written before the deadline
Run five gates on your deal before the inspection window closes

gates.q: Is legal STR use at this address confirmed?
gates.no: Walk, or extend the window in writing

gates.q: Will an insurer write a policy at a price your numbers can carry?
Is real guest capacity at least what the underwriting assumed?
Is the revised base case positive and inside your written buy-box rules?
gates.sub: PA.1 limits: weak case, coverage, minimum cash flow.

gates.q: Do the revised numbers pass the cash test you set in PA.8?

slides.end: All five pass: record the decision, the date, and the reason in one sentence.
slides.notes:
These are the decision rules from the exercise. Run them in order, before the window closes.

Gate one is legal use. If STR use at this address is prohibited or still unresolved, walk, or get the window extended in writing. Don't close on 'probably.'

Gate two is insurance. If no insurer will write a policy at a price your numbers can carry, walk.

Gate three is capacity. If the real number is lower than the underwriting assumed, stop and rerun revenue before you touch anything else.

Gate four is the revised base case. If it's negative, or it breaks a written buy-box rule from PA.1, renegotiate or walk. A budget change or a rule change only counts in writing, with the reason.

Gate five is your own cash test from PA.8. If the revised numbers break it, renegotiate or walk.

If everything passes, write one sentence with the decision, the date, and the reason. Cedar Ridge passed gate four on its final budget, and gate five with $7,265 unallocated.

slides.title: Rerun the PA.4 baseline with your own findings before the window closes
slides.text: Copy the 20-row tracker in PA.9.9 too. Fill in Verified by and Deadline the day you sign, before any findings come in.
rows: Gross booking revenue (change only if capacity changed)
One-time repairs you pay after closing
slides.notes:
Here's your exercise. There are two parts.

First, copy the 20-row diligence tracker from the lesson. It covers permit, transfer, covenants, insurance, flood, capacity, every building system, title, survey, appraisal, and existing bookings. Fill in the Verified by and Deadline columns the day you sign. Do it before any findings come in, so every row already has an owner and a date.

Second, complete this rerun box. The Before column comes straight from your PA.4 package. The After column comes from your tracker.

Only change gross revenue if real capacity changed. Add every new recurring cost to operating costs. Put one-time repairs you'll pay after closing on their own line, and add them to total cash in.

Then run the five gates from the last slide against the After column.

slides.title: Six professionals each confirm one slice of diligence, in writing
rows: Contingency deadlines, written extensions, how to terminate without losing earnest money
STR use for the parcel, permit transfer, occupancy caps, new-application timing
Permitted bedroom count and design capacity of the septic system
Whether the policy can be bound, its conditions and price for your guest count, flood coverage
How the loan is sized after the appraisal, and whether the appraisal includes income analysis
Which liens get paid at closing, what each exception means, whether a survey is required
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms what. I'm not the last word on any of these, and neither are you.

Your attorney or agent owns the calendar. Contingency deadlines, extensions in writing, and how to terminate without losing your earnest money.

The licensing or zoning office owns legal use. Permit transfer, occupancy caps, and how long a new application takes.

The county health department or the septic inspector owns the bedroom count the septic was designed for.

Your insurance agent owns whether the policy can actually be bound, what conditions come with it, and the price for your guest count. Ask about flood at the same time.

Your lender owns loan sizing after the appraisal, and whether the appraisal includes an income analysis.

The title company and your attorney own the liens, the exceptions, and whether you need a survey.

slides.title: Put your diligence clock and owners on paper before the first report arrives
items: Put every contingency deadline from your contract in a calendar, with a reminder two days before each.
Open a property folder and name every file with the date first.
Fill in Verified by and Deadline for all 20 tracker rows.
Look up your address on the FEMA Flood Map Service Center and save a dated copy of the result.
slides.next: Next: PA.10 Entity & Tax Structure Setup. Bring your lender's written answer on lending to an LLC and your insurer's answer on who can be the named insured.
slides.notes:
Four things this week. Each one takes under an hour.

First, put every contingency deadline in a calendar. Add a reminder two days before each one, so you're never deciding on the last afternoon.

Second, open the property folder. Date first in every file name. You'll thank yourself at closing.

Third, fill in the Verified by and Deadline columns for all 20 rows of the tracker.

Fourth, look up your address on the FEMA flood map and save the result with today's date.

Next comes a question people usually answer too late. Whose name goes on the deed and the loan? PA.10 Entity & Tax Structure Setup treats title owner, operator, and tax treatment as three separate choices. Before you watch it, ask your lender whether it lends to an LLC. Ask your insurer who can be the named insured. Get both answers in writing.

slides.notes:
These are the main sources behind this lesson. The full list, including the CPSC vacation rental tips and Airbnb's safety and AirCover pages, is in the PA.9 sources section.

Most of the rules come from the CFPB: the inspection contingency, the difference between an inspector and an appraiser, your right to a copy of the appraisal, and what each title policy covers.

The water and septic guidance comes from the EPA and the CDC. The flood point comes from FEMA.

Each one was checked on September 25, 2026, through a search summary of the official page, because direct fetches were blocked. Before you rely on any of them, open the page yourself. Agencies update these pages, and your state or county may add rules on top.

The Cedar Ridge findings are assumptions for teaching. The baseline figures come from the canonical example.
